paragraphs.source_en: However meritorious his pockmarked face might be, and however useful it might be as material for moral instruction, filthiness is filthiness after all; so from the time my master first came to know the ways of the world, he began to worry over the pockmarks covering his face and tried every possible means to rub out this ugliness. But this was not like old Sōhaku’s sedan chair, which could be thrown away the moment one took a dislike to it. Even today those pockmarks remain plainly visible on his face; and, it is said, my master is somewhat bothered by this plain visibility, so whenever he walks along the street he counts how many pockmarked faces he has met that day. Were the owners of these pockmarked faces men or women, and did he meet them at the Ogawamachi bazaar or in Ueno Park? He records all these details one by one in his diary, firmly convinced that his knowledge of pockmarks is absolutely superior to anyone else’s. The other day, when a friend who had returned from studying overseas came to his house, he even asked him, “Tell me, do Westerners have pockmarks too?” When asked this, his friend said, “Well, how shall I put it?” Then he tilted his head and thought for quite some time before saying, “One hardly sees them.” My master solemnly repeated the question: “Even if one hardly sees them, there are still a few, aren’t there?” The friend replied with a rather indifferent expression, “If there are any, they are among beggars or refuse-pickers. Among educated people, there seem to be none.” My master said, “Is that so? That is a little different from Japan.”

paragraphs.source_en: Following the philosopher’s advice, my master had given up the idea of quarreling with the students of Rakuunkan. After that he shut himself up in his study all day, constantly thinking about something. Perhaps he meant to accept the advice and cultivate his active spirit passively through quiet sitting. But my master is by nature a small-spirited man, and if someone like him spends all day doing nothing but brooding gloomily, naturally no good result can come of it. I rather think it would be far better for him to pawn his books, find a geisha, and learn the Rappabushi tune from her. Still, a perverse man like him would certainly never heed the advice of a cat like me, so I decided to let him do as he pleased. Thus for five or six days I paid him no attention.

paragraphs.source_en: Today is exactly the seventh day since then; among Zen people, a seven-day period is called one shichinichi, and there are many who sit in meditation with tremendous resolve, determined to attain great enlightenment. I thought, “I wonder what has become of my master? Alive? Dead? Surely there must be some conclusion.” So I ambled leisurely from the veranda to the entrance of the study and made a reconnaissance of the movements inside.

paragraphs.source_en: My master’s study is a south-facing six-mat room, and in a spot where the sun often shines there stands a very large low desk. Simply calling it a large desk will not make it understood. It is six feet long, three feet eight inches wide, and its height is in keeping with its general size. Of course it is not a ready-made article, but a rare object specially commissioned from a nearby furniture maker to serve as both desk and bed. Why he had such a desk made to order, and why the idea of sleeping on top of it occurred to him, I have never asked him, so I do not understand in the least. Perhaps it was merely a passing whim of my master’s that caused him to bring in such a massive thing. Or perhaps, out of that habit we so often observe in the mentally ill, of associating two ideas with no relation whatever, he forcibly joined desk and bed together. In any case, it is an eccentric notion. The thing is very unusual; its only defect is that it is useless. I once saw my master taking a nap on this desk, and as he turned over he rolled off onto the veranda. Since then, it seems, this desk has never again been used as a bed.

paragraphs.source_zh: 主人的书斋是朝南的铺六张席子的房间，在阳光经常照射的地方摆有一张很大的矮脚桌。只说是一张大桌子，还不能使人了解。它有六尺长，三尺八寸宽，高度也适合整体的大小。当然这不是现成的制品，而是和附近的家具店交涉后特地让他们制作的书桌与床两用的稀奇之物。为什么要订做这样一张桌子，又为什么产生了要在这上边睡觉的想法，我没有问本人，所以我毫不了解。也许只是由于主人一时的心血来潮，才抬来这样一个庞然大物。说不定是他出于一种我们在精神病患者身上屡见不鲜的、将两个毫不相关的观念联想起来，因而将桌子和床硬扯在一起了。总之，是个古怪的想法。东西是很奇特，唯一的缺点是不适用。我曾经看见过主人在这个桌子上睡午觉，在一翻身的当儿，滚落到廊子上去了。从那以后，好像这张桌子就再也没有当作床用啦。

paragraphs.source_en: In front of the desk lies a thin cushion made of merino cloth, with three holes burned in one spot by cigarette ash. The cotton showing through the holes is a dingy gray-black. Sitting stiffly on this cushion with his back toward me is my master. Around his waist he has wound a gray sash twice, and its two ends droop all the way down to the soles of his feet. Only recently I toyed with that sash with my paws, and at once received a blow on the head. It is not a sash one may casually approach.
